name: Second Plague Wave, "The Pestilence of Children"
summary: The second major plague epidemic (called the Pestilence of Children or Second Pestilence) strikes Europe in 1360-1363, killing primarily children and young adults who had been born after the first plague and lacked immunity. This wave demonstrates that plague is endemic rather than a one-time event; subsequent waves occur in 1369, 1374-1375, 1379-1383, and almost every decade thereafter through the 15th century. Total European population does not recover to pre-1348 levels until 1500-1550.

_quarry.structural_significance: The recurrence of plague is as important as the initial outbreak for social transformation; the demographic deficit persists for a century, keeping wages high, enabling peasant mobility, and transforming the European economy toward labor-saving techniques and livestock (less labor than grain farming); the continuous mortality also shapes late medieval religious culture, the danse macabre, the ars moriendi tradition, and the intense focus on death in art
